target.title: LipVoicer: Generating Speech from Silent Videos Guided by Lip Reading

read.pdf: Fig. 1–4 captions and Tables 1–16 read in text.txt; figure images themselves were not supplied

entries.text: The authors claim LipVoicer is the first lip-to-speech method to use text inferred by a lip-reader as inference-time guidance.
entries.condition: The claim is qualified by 'to the best of our knowledge'; text comes from a pre-trained lip-reading model and guides diffusion through an ASR classifier.
entries.quote:
To the best of our knowledge, LipV oicer is the first method to use text inferred by lip-reading
to enhance lip-to-speech synthesis.

entries.text: Inference predicts text from the silent video, generates mel-spectrograms conditioned on video, applies ASR classifier guidance toward that text, then vocodes the mel-spectrogram.
entries.condition: MelGen is trained without text guidance; the text is predicted by a pre-trained lip-reader and introduced at inference; DiffWave is the paper's vocoder.
entries.quote: We, however, utilize it at inference time.

entries.text: The authors claim best results on LRS2 and LRS3 in both human evaluation and ASR WER, and claim state-of-the-art performance on challenging in-the-wild datasets.
entries.condition: The paper's comparisons cover LRS2 and LRS3; the full comparison excludes ReVISE and SVTS is available only on LRS3.
entries.quote: LipV oicer achieves state-of-the-art results for highly challenging in-the-wild datasets.

entries.text: The authors claim the lip-reading and ASR modules can be replaced with improved versions without retraining LipVoicer.
entries.condition: This is a stated modularity advantage of separating MelGen from the lip-to-text and ASR components.

entries.text: LRS2 test set contains 1,243 videos.
entries.condition: LRS2 full test split; the paper trains on that dataset's pretrain+train splits and evaluates on the full unseen test data split.

entries.text: LRS3 test split contains 1,452 videos; its train and pre-train portions contain 9,000 speakers and 151,000 videos across 430 hours.
entries.unit: test videos; speakers; train+pretrain videos; hours
entries.condition: LRS3 dataset statistics; test videos are evaluated on the full unseen test split.

entries.text: LipVoicer is trained separately on pretrain+train for LRS2 and LRS3; dataset transcriptions are not used as direct LipVoicer text guidance during training or inference.
entries.condition: The paper separately states that the ASR classifier is fine-tuned with ground-truth text targets; see t9.

entries.text: MelGen's diffusion denoiser is trained to generate mel-spectrograms conditioned on video without the text modality.
entries.condition: Classifier-free conditioning uses the face image and mouth-region video; ASR text guidance is added only during inference.
entries.quote:
At first, we train MelGen, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models ( DDPM) model
trained to generate a mel-spectrogram waveform x conditioned on the video V without the text
modality.

entries.text: The modified ASR is fine-tuned with CTC using diffusion-noised training mel-spectrograms as inputs and ground-truth text as targets.
entries.condition: ASR fine-tuning uses the LRS2 and LRS3 train+pretrain splits; the paper reports Adam at learning rate 1e−4 and batch size 256 as 4 accumulated mini-batches of 64.
entries.quote: the target is the ground truth text.

entries.text: Video preprocessing uses 25-fps video, a randomly selected 224×224 full-face frame, and grayscale 96×96 mouth crops; training uses random 88×88 crops and horizontal flips with probability 0.5, while inference uses a center crop without flipping.
entries.unit: fps; pixels; pixels; pixels; flip probability
entries.condition: The face image is randomly selected from full-face frames; brightness and color augmentation are also applied during training.

entries.text: Audio preprocessing extracts 16-kHz training speech, peak-normalizes to 0.9, uses 640-sample STFT window/transform length and a 160-sample hop, then computes 80 mel bins from 20 Hz to 8 kHz and log-compresses values clipped at 1e−5.
entries.unit: Hz; amplitude; samples; samples; mel bins; Hz; Hz; magnitude floor
entries.condition: The paper says log-mels are linearly mapped to roughly [−1,1] using global minimum and maximum values across the training split; repository implementation differs (t71).

entries.text: MelGen is trained for 1,000,000 mini-batches of 16 videos with Adam at learning rate 2e−4 and no learning-rate schedule; conditioning dropout probability is 0.2.
entries.unit: mini-batches; videos/batch; learning rate; conditioning-drop probability
entries.condition: The paper reports four NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPUs; training examples cover one second (100 mel frames and 25 video frames).

entries.text: MelGen uses a 400-step linear diffusion schedule from β1=0.0001 to βT=0.02, with 12 residual layers of 512 channels; the paper's waveform vocoder is conditional DiffWave with 50 diffusion steps.
entries.unit: diffusion steps; β1; βT; residual layers; channels; vocoder steps
entries.condition: MelGen uses an 80-channel mel-spectrogram representation; the DiffWave vocoder is trained on LRS3 training audio only.
entries.quote:
Using the notations from Kong et al. (2021), the diffusion process has
T = 400 steps.

entries.text: Selected LRS2 inference settings are w1=1.8, w2=1.7, and tASR=230 diffusion steps.
entries.unit: guidance weights; guidance weights; diffusion step
entries.condition: Selected by a hyperparameter grid search and listening tests; the paper does not state which split or samples were used for selection.

entries.text: Selected LRS3 inference settings are w1=2, w2=1.5, and tASR=270 diffusion steps.
entries.unit: guidance weights; guidance weights; diffusion step
entries.condition: Selected by a hyperparameter grid search and listening tests; the paper does not state which split or samples were used for selection.

entries.text: Selected GRID inference settings are w1=2.6, w2=0.7, and tASR=300 diffusion steps.
entries.unit: guidance weights; guidance weights; diffusion step
entries.condition: Selected by a hyperparameter grid search and listening tests; the paper does not state which split or samples were used for selection.

entries.text: The Ma et al. (2023) lip-reader has reported WER of 14.6% on LRS2 and 19.1% on LRS3 against ground-truth text.
entries.condition: Lip-reader performance used for predicting text at inference; the sentence does not specify the exact evaluation split or decoding settings.
entries.quote:
It achieves a WER rate of 14.6% and 19.1% with
respect to the ground truth text, respectively.

entries.unit: speakers; utterances/speaker; training speakers; test speakers

entries.text: The authors could not include ReVISE in the full comparisons because public test files were unavailable and training was computationally expensive; ReVISE reported using 32 GPUs.
entries.condition: This limits the direct baseline comparison; the authors instead ran a separate ASR comparison on LRS3.

entries.text: On LRS3 using the reproduced ReVISE ASR, LipVoicer WER is 33.2% versus ReVISE's reported 33.9%.
entries.condition: LRS3 comparison using the ASR from Hsu et al. (2022); authors could not reproduce the ASR's reported 5.6% ground-truth WER and obtained 6.4% instead.
entries.quote:
While we are uncertain of the source of the degraded performance, we evaluated LipV oicer
using this ASR and achieved WER score of 33.2% on LRS3, whereas ReVISE reported 33.9%.

entries.text: The Hsu et al. (2022) ASR is reported at 5.6% WER on LRS3 ground-truth test videos, while the authors obtain 6.4% on the same data.
entries.condition: LRS3 ground-truth test videos; same ASR family used for the separate LipVoicer–ReVISE comparison.
entries.quote: we only managed to achieve 6.4% on the same

entries.text: SVTS comparisons are limited to LRS3 because the authors supplied only LRS3 generated test files; its code was not open-sourced.
entries.condition: Applies to objective and human comparisons; no LRS2 SVTS result is reported.

entries.text: The authors concede an intelligibility–naturalness/synchronization trade-off: ASR guidance can make speech less natural and can cause synchronization lapses when predicted text poorly overlaps ground truth.
entries.condition: They also observe that MelGen without ASR guidance sometimes sounds more natural, while ASR guidance substantially improves WER.

entries.text: The authors identify misrepresentation/manipulation risk: bad-faith actors could inject misleading text into the lip-reading-guided system; mitigation is beyond the paper's scope.
entries.condition: The paper also notes the potential positive use of restoring missing or corrupted speech in important videos.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds or repeated independent training runs for MelGen, the fine-tuned ASR, or stochastic speech generation.
entries.condition: No seed/repetition count is supplied for headline LRS2/LRS3 WER, synchronization, or MOS results.

entries.text: The paper says test videos are unseen but does not establish whether train/test partitions are speaker-disjoint or report speaker-overlap counts for LRS2/LRS3.
entries.condition: Unseen-video status is explicit; speaker-level independence is not stated for these benchmark test comparisons.

entries.text: The paper says guidance weights were selected by grid search and listening tests but does not identify the selection/validation split, samples, listener count, or whether any test data informed tuning.
entries.condition: Applies to the selected w1, w2 and tASR settings for LRS2, LRS3 and GRID.

entries.text: The paper names Ma et al. (2023) as the WER evaluation ASR but does not specify the evaluator's decoding/LM configuration or the text-normalization rules used for its WER scores.
entries.condition: The paper reports that Ma et al. (2023) achieves 1.5% LRS2 and 1.0% LRS3 WER on the ground-truth test sets, but does not document evaluation-time normalization or decoding settings for generated audio.

entries.text: No chance-level or random-output reference is reported for WER, synchronization, or the four MOS dimensions.
entries.condition: MOS is collected on a 1–5 scale and includes ground-truth speech as an anchor, but no chance-level interpretation is defined.

entries.text: The paper does not define what the ± values in MOS tables represent (for example, standard deviation, standard error, or confidence interval).
entries.condition: Applies to Tables 1, 2, 13 and 16; number of samples and annotators is reported, but uncertainty construction is not.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge non-negligible noise in human-rater scores and respond with multiple raters per sample and filtering based on ground-truth ratings.
entries.condition: Main LRS2/LRS3 human evaluation; each annotator rated all methods for a given sample.

entries.text: The authors argue that PESQ and STOI are intrusive and unsuitable as primary lip-to-speech metrics because a valid generated voice need not reproduce the original audio signal or pitch.
entries.condition: They provide PESQ/STOI scores in Appendix D for completeness but exclude those measures from the main report.

entries.text: Repository data loading seeds Python's random module with 1234 before shuffling mouth-crop files and using Python random choices; the MelGen training script does not set a Torch or NumPy global seed.
entries.condition: Code-only seed detail; paper reports random frame/crop choices but no seed or RNG-specific reproducibility condition.

entries.text: Repository MelGen training periodically generates three samples from LipVoicerDataset('test') at checkpoint intervals (default 10,000 iterations), providing test-split qualitative monitoring during training; the paper does not describe this use of test data.
entries.condition: The code calls generation when saving a checkpoint; it does not state that checkpoints are selected by test metrics.

entries.text: The repository ASR fine-tuning config trains on LRS3 pretrain+trainval and uses LRS3 test as its evaluation dataset; the ASR fit routine evaluates periodically, a condition not stated in the paper.
entries.condition: The paper says the modified ASR is fine-tuned on train+pretrain splits but does not disclose test-split evaluation during ASR fitting or specify a validation split.

entries.text: Repository normalise_mel uses a fixed log(1e−5) floor and fixed linear scale to map values, rather than computing the training-split global minimum and maximum stated in the paper; this is an implementation/text discrepancy.
entries.condition: The fixed mapping is applied in the MelGen dataset loader; the repository's wav2mel script stores raw log-mels before dataset normalization.

entries.text: SyncNet found GRID-4S and TCD-TIMIT-LS offsets centered near zero, with some samples off by one video frame (±40 ms).
entries.condition: Dataset-level SyncNet analysis, not reported as test-only: GRID-4S (4 speakers; small vocabulary/artificial grammar) and TCD-TIMIT-LS (3 professionally trained lip speakers; larger-vocabulary real English sentences); SyncNet uses 25 FPS video and 16 kHz audio at 40 ms resolution. No decoding/LM or seed specified.

entries.text: Lip2Wav offsets were centered around −200 to −250 ms for chess and around −80 ms for other speakers.
entries.condition: Dataset-level SyncNet analysis (not reported as test-only) on five Lip2Wav YouTube-lecture speakers: chem, chess, dl, eh, hs. No vocabulary size, decoding/LM, or seed specified.

entries.text: The evaluation frontend searches 61 audio shifts from −300 to +300 ms in 10 ms steps and selects the shift minimizing normalized-mel MSE before scoring.
entries.value: 61 shifts; −300 to +300 in 10 ms steps; minimum-MSE shift
entries.condition: Generated/reference audio pairs at evaluation; mel window 640, hop 160, channel-normalized. Dataset/test-set, speakers, vocabulary, decoding/LM, and seeds are not specified for the frontend procedure.

entries.text: Alignment-sensitive scores fall sharply under small synthetic shifts: at 8 ms STOI/ESTOI are 0.770/0.708 and MCD is 15.605, versus 1.000/1.000 and 0.000 at 0 ms.
entries.condition: Synthetic offset test on two copies of the same GRID-4S audio (bbaf2n), with one copy shifted; no listener subjects, vocabulary or decoding/LM, and no seeds reported.

entries.text: The subjective MOS protocol used 12 volunteers, 10 randomly selected Lip2Wav chem test samples, and four versions per sample; volunteers rated intelligibility and naturalness.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav chem test set (speaker chem); each volunteer rated VCA-GAN, SLTS, SLTS w/ dis, and real voice on intelligibility and naturalness. Vocabulary details, ASR decoding/LM, and seeds not specified.

entries.text: Lip2Wav chem MOS (intelligibility/naturalness) was 3.250/2.042 for VCA-GAN, 3.633/1.858 for SLTS, 4.483/4.267 for SLTS w/ dis, and 4.808/4.975 for real voice; reported intervals are 95% CIs.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav chem test set; 12 volunteers rated 10 random samples in four versions. Table reports 95% confidence intervals computed from a t-distribution. Vocabulary details, decoding/LM, and seeds not specified.

entries.text: Associated voice-face representation learning transfers speech-identity knowledge to face-based speaker embeddings (FSE), allowing face images to control unseen-speaker voice characteristics without reference speech.
entries.condition: Zero-shot inference for unseen speakers using a target face image; no reference utterance required; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: The first video frame is encoded into the target speaker's FSE; the embedding is mapped from 512 to 256 dimensions and concatenated with upsampled 512-dimensional linguistic content representations.
entries.condition: Silent video of target speaker; face-image conditioning; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: A non-autoregressive 5-layer Conformer predicts mel spectrograms (256-D attention, four heads, 31 × 1 convolution); a postnet converts them to linear spectrograms and Griffin-Lim reconstructs the waveform.
entries.condition: GRID acoustic targets at 16 kHz; mel-to-linear postnet and Griffin-Lim waveform reconstruction; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: GRID has 33 speakers with 1K videos per speaker; each utterance contains six context-independent words.
entries.condition: GRID dataset; constrained six-word utterances.

entries.text: Twenty GRID speakers (10 female, 10 male) were split per speaker into 90% train, 5% development, and 5% seen test; the remaining 13 speakers form the unseen test set.
entries.condition: GRID; seen-speaker train/development/test plus held-out unseen-speaker test; six-word vocabulary; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: The speech identity encoder was trained on VoxCeleb2 and the face identity encoder pretrained on VGGFace2; 5,994 speakers common to both datasets supplied paired speech-image cross-modal training data.
entries.condition: Voice-face representation pretraining, separate from GRID Lip2Speech test speakers.

entries.text: On unseen speakers, the face-conditioned Proposed system reports STOI 0.589, ESTOI 0.389, and EER 36.72.
entries.condition: Unseen GRID test: remaining 13 speakers; six context-independent words per utterance; face FSE, no reference audio; no LM or seeds reported.

entries.text: The reference-speech-conditioned Proposed Speech system has substantially lower unseen-speaker EER than face-conditioned Proposed, so the reported speaker-similarity result favors reference-audio conditioning.
entries.value: Proposed Speech EER 26.57 vs Proposed EER 36.72
entries.condition: Unseen-speaker GRID test; Proposed Speech uses a target-speaker reference utterance while Proposed uses face FSE.

entries.text: RobustL2S maps AV-HuBERT visual SSL features to HuBERT speech SSL features as disentangled speech content, rather than directly predicting mel spectrograms.
entries.condition: Lip-to-speech representation mapping; AV-HuBERT visual encoder and HuBERT speech encoder.

entries.text: The non-autoregressive Seq2Seq decoder predicts every speech representation simultaneously; its encoder and decoder use feed-forward transformer blocks with self-attention and 1D convolutions.
entries.condition: Lip SSL representations are mapped to speech SSL representations; encoder includes a transposed convolution to align video and audio rates.

questions.q: What is the claimed methodological novelty, and when is text used?
questions.answer: The claimed novelty is inference-time use of text inferred by a lip-reader: MelGen is trained video-conditioned without text, then an ASR classifier guides diffusion toward the predicted text at inference.

questions.q: What are the headline LRS2/LRS3 objective and human-evaluation results, and what conditions govern them?
questions.answer: On the full unseen test splits, LipVoicer reports WER 17.8% on LRS2 and 21.4% on LRS3, with objective-metric rows in Tables 3–4. Human MOS uses 50 random samples per dataset and 16 raters per sample; uncertainty notation is undefined.

questions.q: Does the evidence establish an unqualified state-of-the-art comparison?
questions.answer: The paper claims best results against its included LRS2/LRS3 baselines, but ReVISE is omitted from full comparisons and SVTS is evaluated only on LRS3; the separate ReVISE-ASR comparison is not directly matched because the reproduced ASR differs from the reported ground-truth WER.

questions.q: What evaluation or reproducibility conditions remain unclear or differ in code?
questions.answer: The paper omits seeds, speaker-overlap auditing, hyperparameter-selection data, WER decoding/text normalization, chance-level references, and the meaning of MOS ± values. The repository uses the test split for qualitative MelGen checkpoint samples and ASR evaluation, and its fixed mel normalization differs from the paper's split-global normalization description.

questions.q: Which author-acknowledged limitations or risks are explicit?
questions.answer: The authors acknowledge ASR-guidance trade-offs in naturalness and synchronization, noise in human scores, the limits of their ReVISE/SVTS comparisons, and potential speech misrepresentation through injected misleading text.
